Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette: Lani, a second-generation Samoan American, was twenty when the weeks of being followed by a stranger bled into outright terror. It began with misplaced keys and a photograph left on her kitchen counter, but it rapidly escalated into a coordinated campaign of surveillance. He learned her routines, waited outside her apartment complex, and finally cornered her in the dim concrete of a parking garage, his face inches from hers as he whispered that he would always be watching. The violation was absolute. In the months that followed, Lani did not just remember the garage; she internalized it as proof that her life had been destroyed. The safety of her former existence felt irrevocably shattered, replaced by a conviction that the world was a dangerous place where threat could materialize without warning. This belief manifested as a relentless, bodily need to be on guard all the time. Her eyes constantly tracked exits in crowded rooms, her shoulders tensed at the screech of tires, and she mapped every possible route home with meticulous, anxious precision. When the sliding glass doors of her audit firm’s lobby hissed open, Lani’s breath would catch, instantly pulling her back to the cold concrete of the garage. That visceral memory, combined with her certainty that her life was ruined, directly funneled into how she punished herself and structured her days. Because she was convinced the world remained unsafe and that her past was irreparably broken, Lani told herself she deserved to suffer because of what happened. She reasoned that if she could not protect herself then, she had no right to claim comfort now. This self-inflicted penance dictated her avoidance of going out; she stopped answering invitations, canceled plans, and told friends she was working. She actively avoided positive events, refusing to attend gallery openings or birthday dinners, convinced that feeling happy or hopeful would be a betrayal of the trauma. Her firm’s glass-walled compliance office became the stage where these habits calcified. During financial reviews, she would abruptly pack her laptop and leave early rather than risk the evening commute. At work, she declined client site visits, choosing instead to process paperwork in isolation, which slowly isolated her from her team and drew managerial concern. Over the last six months, the pattern tightened relentlessly. Her certainty that the world was dangerous kept her need to be on guard all the time dialed to a constant hum, which in turn reinforced her belief that her life was destroyed, leaving no room for anything that might make her feel hopeful. Every avoided outing and every hour spent in self-reproach felt like evidence that she was paying her debt, cementing her isolation. Now, sitting in her therapist’s office for the first time, Lani faces the collapse of her career and her social world. An auditor’s role requires presence and mobility, both of which have evaporated under the weight of her avoidance. She has come to this session because her performance review is approaching, but she is most afraid that stepping back into the world will once again place her in the line of fire, and she secretly hopes to learn how to walk through a crowded street without feeling the walls closing in.
